title: Jelly Roll Morton, Chicago and Joe Oliver's band
summary: Kimball joins Morton's band, Bill lends Morton fare, and in Chicago visits Oliver and lists his band.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Before I come home. You didn't tell about Jelly. That was around St. Louis, was it?

Well, that's around St. Louis. Only one I know in the band, the Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll was on the road there. He had an old bus. And I was living out on Phoenix with old man Kimball. Old man Kimball, the bass player. So he said, well, Billy, I'm going to join Jelly. I ain't doing nothing. I'm going to join Jelly Roll. And from there, make a trip with him. I said, well, Pop, when you're going back home? He said, well, anywhere is my home now. My son is raised now. That's a little bit of Kimball, a banjo player. He said, my son is raised now. I don't care. Anywhere is my home. So he joined Jelly Roll, him and Dawes, several other fellas I know. Harry Dolls and all that. They joined Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll come from Chicago over there to pick up a bunch. So I said, well, I'm not going right now. I said, I'm going to stick you up in Charlotte Crescent and make this money. I said, Papa Foster said, look, don't you go before you stay here. You stay right here. Stay right here. So finally they made a tour about, say about four months or so. They come right back to St. Louis. And they come out to St. Louis. They was down. That's why the boys jumped down from Jelly Roll. So I got kind of funny myself about St. Louis. So Jelly said, Billy, I said, what do you say, Fred? His name is Fred Mouton. I'll call him Jelly. I said, well, anytime you come to Chicago, you look me up. Here's my address. I said, sure, I'll do that. He said, I'm going. He said, so Jelly was kind of a smart guy. He was all pigeon-toed stuff. He was pigeon-toed. Kind of smart old red guy. So I brought him up. He's come out of the house and talked to me. He said, what do I want you to do for me? Before he asked me for any money for transportation, he put that question to me about coming to Chicago. I said, I want you to give me an advance me back to Chicago. I said, you should ask me that in front. Go and come jive me like that, you know. I said, you know, we're all home for it. He said, you be back down by Ironton after a while. I said, it's home, Ironton. Ironton, Louisiana right down. His home was not in Northern. What town? Ironton. About 12 miles from here. Down the road. Down the river farther or which way? That little road used to go down. They don't run down. Round, round, finest down that way. Little town they call it Ironton. That's Jolly Road home.
Jolly Road and Jimbo. Jimbo. That's the damn one of the cutouts. Jimco and all that. All that.

Down toward Buras. Down that way. That's down that way. Yeah. So I told him, I said, well, yeah, sure. I'll give you a fare. Went to the station. Went to the station. He got his ticket and everything. And I gave him two extra dollars. Because I was planning on going to Chicago anyway. You know? Yeah. So I said, well, before I could go to Chicago, I'm going to, you know, straighten things out where I want to live at. In Chicago. So that's the break I had. So I went to Chicago. Over to Jolly. I mean, I went on to give Jolly his money. And Jolly got home. He wrote me back a nice letter and everything. And two weeks after that, Jolly sent me $10 bill. Yeah. And any time I'm coming to Chicago, I'd be welcome to his house. Jolly was welcome. He said, well, find home and everything. But at that time, he was down. I was pushing travel on the road. And have a bunch of men in stock. Something got to happen. I said, hell. I was a booking agent like that. I said, them days was different from now. I said, you had 12, 15 pieces in the band. I said, take your 12, 15 men's. It's tough. You know, it's bust. So he sent me a $10 bill. So I told Foster, I said, Papa, I'm going to make me trip over to Chicago. I'm not going to say. Not Papa, old man Kimball. I said, I'm going to make me trip over to Chicago. I'm not going to say. I said, this guy over there for all the visits. Because I've never been to Chicago. I said, he said, okay. Well, you must come back. I said, okay. I'm coming back. So when I got to Chicago, first one was at the station meeting. It was General. Nice place to stay and everything. See? So he wanted me to join his band. I said, I'm going to go back to St. Louis. I said, I'm going back to St. Louis. I'm working. I'm going back to St. Louis. I said, I'm going to come here for a week or so. Let's see how Chicago is. So that's when I met an alma twy. I said, what you doing here in the name? I said, I'm working. What you doing here, man? How long you been here? I said, I got here about two months ago. He said, who you playing with? I said, over St. Louis. I heard about it. You playing trombone? I said, yeah. We all used to play in the brass band. I got me and an alma twy. I said, yeah, I'm playing trombone. He said, man, come on around here. Come on around here. Old Creole boy. We went on around here. Went to Joe Oliver house. That's why I was talking. Mr. Oliver and Oliver's preak's dinner. So Joe said, don't you want for nothing? Don't you want your little son? He said, don't you want for nothing? Ora was living right next door. I said, where's Ora? I said, he's over there, a tramp. He said, Joe, a tramp. He can't make it here, Bill. He can't make it here. You know how to read, can't you? I said, you know. That's my best house, Joe. He said, well, Ora can't make it here. I said, no, I'm poor boy. He had a big goal. He didn't help you play. He said, like that. He didn't help you play. Now, you helped him. He said, I'm going to help him. I got him on full saxophone. He said, let's not play saxophone. He ain't doing good on full saxophone. He was carrying through. So, who he had in his bunch. He was Simeone, violin, and clarinet, and saxophone. And Albert Nicholas, and Bonnie. That's the head of his band. He had King, was on trumpet. Nora Duce was on trombone. No, Nora wasn't Nora. Nora Duce wasn't on trombone. Nora was spinning across the street. It wasn't Nora.
It was with Hines and Dickerson, I guess.

That's right. And then Paul Barbrae was on drums. And Russell's on piano. Russell. Yeah, Lou Russell. I just remember how many they had. They had a big band. Was George Field in Chicago then? George Field, that's right.

On trombone. That's what was right. You're right about that, sir. So, that time, Lewis was in Chicago then, doing good. That's when they had to broke up. See, they had to broke up. I know why they broke up. See, Lewis broke up on kind of there. Lewis was a young man, and Joe was, that was Joe's girlfriend. So, Lewis got in there in Tukli, in Maryland, and that's quite natural. They had to separate, you understand? Yeah. So, that's why. So, Nora, me and Nora were separated together with old man McCollum, see, here in New Orleans.
